Other elements of apparent strangeness, such as color changes and the impression of the UFO's altitude dropping in a jerky or stepped fashion, are classic observations of Venus at low elevation through atmospheric layers that create color changes. The initial misinterpretation (failure to recognize it due to the glow and colors) is the origin of the error in distance estimation and ultimately the illusion of a following sphere. The whole reinforces each other in strangeness. The strong coherence of appearance and position in the sky with Venus leaves no doubt. The few elements that might contradict this (final eastward movement) cannot be considered because they come from only one witness out of the four, in singularity or contradiction with the other three. Finally, none of the witnesses has Venus was observed for over 30 minutes, despite clear skies and Venus being in the direction of observation, which should have been a key reference point for locating the UFO. Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as A: observations of Venus.

summary: Nighttime observations from a vehicle of a luminous ball moving close to the ground in successive jumps: mistaken for the Moon at sunrise.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its website: www.cnes-geipan.fr. Its publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This observation, previously classified as C and named LOUHANS (71) 1980, is part of a group of cases recently re-examined. On April 7, 1980, around 2:00 AM, two people (Passenger T1 and Driver T2) traveling on the D13 departmental road a few kilometers from Saint-Usuge (71) spotted a reddish-orange light at a very low altitude. This light was located approximately above the Seille River and appeared to be moving along the waterway. On the D178 at a place called "Varennes," the UFO was seen as a sphere, moving close to the ground in successive hops. The witnesses then saw the sphere fall and come to rest on one side of the road. The driver stopped, then, panicking, reversed and turned around. As a car approached from the opposite direction, the witnesses saw the sphere gain altitude and disappear. The witnesses went to the gendarmerie. The observation lasted approximately 10 minutes. This case is consistent (two witnesses), and the description of the observed UFO is quite precise. The sincerity and credibility of the witnesses have never been questioned (see the investigation notes). The initial classification as Category C does not appear to be justified at all. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the Moon at sunrise. The Moon was indeed rising along the axis indicated by the witnesses. The perceived movement of the UFO corresponds to the typical illusions created by a celestial body: the UFO follows the moving witnesses along a parallel trajectory; this is the illusion of the following sphere. The direction of the celestial body is, of course, absolutely fixed. When the witness's car follows a roughly constant heading, the celestial body appears stationary relative to the vehicle and moves across the landscape. Since the witness does not see the celestial body but a UFO (Unidentified Flying Object) and considers it to be at a close distance, this movement along the landscape is perceived as the UFO moving parallel to the vehicle, reproducing the stop-and-go motion; the perception of the UFO's movement is introduced by its (apparent) movement along the landscape. In the total absence of landscape (sea, desert), the illusion does not occur or is minimal. If the landscape landmarks are close, the celestial body moves quickly behind them; if they are far away, the movement, and therefore the perceived speed of the UFO's movement, is less pronounced. The mere alternation of more or less close landmarks in the landscape is enough for the witness to perceive the UFO's movements as jerky, jumping (moving in jumps). Similarly, the notion of the UFO's height relative to the landscape below is relative; an alternation of landscape heights (poorly recognized) can induce a perception of alternating absolute heights of the UFO, also contributing to the notion of the UFO's jerky movement. Another phenomenon of the celestial body's movement can be created by its variation in light intensity, itself caused by the evolution of the atmospheric veil in front of the celestial body (the sky not being completely clear). This variation is logically interpreted by the witness as a change in the UFO's distance (towards them or away from them) at speeds often described as lightning-fast, particularly during its flight and final disappearance. This flight in distance is then logically described as a flight across the sky or "a gain in altitude," and the witness, of course, neither sees nor describes any change in position in elevation or azimuth (indeed, these are fixed). Here, the witness says the sphere rose at high speed, veering to the right relative to our direction of travel. Indeed, previously the UFO was following the witnesses and had a trajectory parallel to their right; the final movement of the UFO is logically perceived as a departure to the right, thus changing its trajectory. It is worth noting the state of stress and panic experienced by the witnesses: upon panicking, the vehicle moved backward (T1). It is not the witnesses' visual perception that is at issue, but rather their interpretation of their observation based on their feelings (fatigue, night driving, panic). Consequently, GEIPAN classifies the case as UFO A: observation linked to a misinterpretation of the moon at sunrise.

summary: Observation of a white ball rising into the sky, then moving horizontally at very high speed.
description: On April 5, 1980, at approximately 10:45 PM, a witness observed a luminous white ball rising erratically in the sky, leaving a white trail behind it. After ascending, the object moved horizontally at very high speed before disappearing. The investigation failed to identify the observed phenomenon.

summary: Observation of a bright, stationary ball with a noise of air movement.
description: On April 2, 1980, at approximately 11:30 PM, several people observed a luminous sphere in the sky, shaped like a rugby ball. This stationary object remained visible for 20 minutes. It then moved very slowly, accompanied by a whirring sound, described by witnesses as a fan noise. The sphere moved off to the west. The observation continued for almost an hour before being abandoned by the witnesses. No further reports were collected regarding this phenomenon, for which we lack information. The hypothesis of a light helicopter flying at night is consistent with the eyewitness accounts and should not be ruled out, although it has not been verified.

summary: Long observations by four witnesses in a car of the movement of a very bright circular phenomenon in the sky and its disappearance towards the West: observation of Venus at sunset.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as A, B, C, or D, which are now being re-examined to refine the conclusions. This re-examination takes into account new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years. Sometimes, this re-examination results in a change of classification. This observation, previously classified as D and named SAINT-VALLIER (26) 1980, is one of a group of cases recently re-examined (see the investigation report). During a journey, several people in two cars observed a circular luminous phenomenon moving westward in the sky. The UAP was described as a very bright, colored sphere (phosphorescent white, orange, red, according to witnesses) with green, foot-shaped reflections. Once everyone arrived at the same location, they continued their observations until the UAP disappeared behind the mountains to the northwest. The observations lasted between 5 and 20 minutes. The witnesses most likely observed Venus. The significant duration of the observation is typical of this type of mistaken identity. The observation took place to the northwest or west at a low angular elevation, which corresponds well to the location of Venus at the time of the observation, which was around 6 degrees of elevation, to the west-northwest. The appearance of the UAP, primarily described as white, point-like, and very bright, perfectly matches the hypothesis. The variations in the accounts of some witnesses regarding this appearance reflect the fact that Venus was very low on the horizon and subject to atmospheric turbulence that could temporarily and randomly alter its brightness, producing brief color effects (red, green), but also producing strong flashes, which the witnesses described as "lights on foot." The perception of the UFO's rapid movement is explained by the witnesses' travel in a car. The unrecognized celestial body moved along and behind the vehicle and was perceived as a following UFO. Other perceived rapid movements, but with the witness stationary, resulted from the decrease in the celestial body's brightness (thickness of the atmospheric veil), which the witness logically interpreted as movement away from the UFO. The perceived slow movement of the UAP (Unidentified Aerial Phenomenon) does indeed correspond to the setting of Venus, and its disappearance to Venus setting behind the Forez mountains. The only element that could limit this hypothesis would be the presence of cloud cover preventing Venus from being seen that evening. However, given the only available information being a generally clear sky (2/8) at 35 km, and considering the strong correlation with Venus, the probability that it was another phenomenon with cloud cover obscuring Venus is very low. In conclusion, GEIPAN classifies the case as A, indicating a very probable observation of the planet Venus.

summary: Observation of a triangular flying object with a wingspan of 50 meters, no noise, variable speed.
description: On March 27, 1980, around 10 p.m., a driver and his passenger spotted a dark, triangular mass in the sky. Flashing red and white lights at each end indicated the object's size: according to the witness, it was 50 meters across. The craft, initially stationary, then moved, slowly tilting while remaining 50 meters above both the ground and the car. Gaining altitude, the craft then tilted to the right and disappeared into the sky at a considerable speed. During the four to five minutes of observation, with the windows closed, no unusual noises were heard. No further information has been gathered about this phenomenon, which remains unexplained.

summary: Probable observation of the planet Venus
description: On March 25, 1980, starting at 9:50 PM, several military personnel observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon for an hour. A yellowish sphere, larger than a star, emitted strong beams of light. It was observed in the west, slightly above the horizon, though its precise angular position was not known. A star chart at that time showed Venus in the west, approximately 11 arcseconds above the horizon, with a magnitude of -4.22. Sirius was also clearly visible with a magnitude of -1.45, but the witnesses were likely misled by the observation of Venus.

summary: Observation of luminous phenomena identified as being spotlights.
description: On March 23, 1980, at 10:20 PM, several people alerted the police: they had observed unexplained luminous phenomena occurring at the base of the "Mont Caume" terrestrial television relay tower. Upon arriving at the site immediately, and during subsequent investigations on the following evenings, it was determined that the luminous phenomena originated from newly installed signal lights at the foot of the tower. Furthermore, the police discovered that other luminous effects seen from this location were in fact simply the streetlights of surrounding villages and the headlights of passing vehicles. At that time, these signal lights were frequently obscured and disrupted by fog and adverse weather conditions.

summary: OBSERVATION OF A LUMINOUS OBJECT.
description: On March 17, 1980, at 8:40 PM, three people observed a very bright object moving slowly from south to north. This object was circular in shape. This observation was not confirmed by police officers who repeatedly looked at the sky in that direction. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon, for which we lack details.

summary: Observation by three witnesses of the silent evolutions of a luminous yellow-orange mass in the night sky: strange phenomenon of medium or strong consistency.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case, previously classified as D and named EGUILLE (L') (17) 16.03.1980 (but also known as ROYAN (17) 1980), is part of a set of cases recently re-examined (see the investigation report). On March 16, 1980, around 12:30 a.m., three witnesses were intrigued by the presence of a luminous, yellow-orange mass in the low, overcast night sky. For 45 minutes, despite coming and going (particularly to alert the police), the witnesses followed the silent movements of the phenomenon. It quickly disappeared between Marennes and Rochefort (Charente-Maritime). A sketch depicting the movement of the unidentified flying object (UFO) and the surrounding landscape is attached to the official report, along with a site plan and an annotated photographic plate showing the UFO's position. No other witness statements were collected. Only two hypotheses were considered, studied, and investigated; these were ultimately quite similar. The hypothesis of the impact of a spotlight on the lower cloud layer from a poacher (in a boat or on foot) fishing for elvers (official fishermen never go out on Sundays) is plausible given the privileged position of the witnesses, located in the immediate vicinity and observing along the axis of the Seudre River, where this fishing takes place. The fishermen use powerful spotlights which, when aimed skyward, can create this striking appearance of a shard on the lower cloud layer. The circular shape, distorted by perspective, the small luminous tail described by witness 1, and the size estimates given by the witnesses are all characteristics compatible with this hypothesis. However, it is undermined by four main factors: the color of the spotlight, which is white and not orange-yellow; the brightness of the UFO, described as very strong, even dazzling, by all three witnesses. Witness 1, for example, describes the surrounding landscape as if it were broad daylight, which is strictly impossible to produce with a spotlight hitting clouds, even low-altitude ones. Consider the risk a poacher would take by leaving their spotlight pointed skyward, making them easily detectable by the authorities. One might also wonder why a poacher would amuse themselves with their spotlight, moving it back and forth in the sky for 45 minutes. The other hypothesis, involving a nightclub spotlight, is plausible, as is the poacher's spotlight, given the observation angle (direction of a coastal area), the shape, dimensions, and the small luminous tail described by Witness 1. The movements described by the witnesses, as well as the yellow-orange color, are also consistent with this hypothesis, as is the date (Saturday night/Sunday morning). However, there is data that invalidates this hypothesis. In particular, we will focus on the brightness of the UFO, described as very strong, even dazzling, by all three witnesses. Witness 1, for example, described the surrounding landscape as being illuminated as if it were broad daylight, which is inconsistent with a spotlight shining on clouds, even low ones. It is off-season, and no establishment capable of using this type of spotlight is open. The distances are too great for it to have been a spotlight used by a local establishment, unless we imagine a nearby, local device, but it is too late for any verification to be carried out on site. Therefore, there is no hypothesis with sufficient probability to explain the observation. In terms of consistency, although all witnesses were interviewed at the Gendarmerie and the resulting report is fairly complete (maps and photographic record), important data is missing, such as azimuth readings for each witness (only Witness 1 provided this information) and elevation angles of the UFO. In the current GEIPAN methodology, the present level of strangeness and consistency necessitates conducting a field investigation with the witness for a reconstruction and a cognitive interview. This latter process is likely to positively and negatively impact the assessment of both strangeness and consistency. However, it is not feasible for a case revisited so long after the event. Therefore, the evaluation of this case is conducted according to the current criteria for considering strangeness and consistency (see GEIPAN news /index.php?id=181&no_cache=1&tx_ttnews[backPid]=211&tx_ttnews[tt_news]=209) as if the field investigation had been carried out and had been completely neutral (no additional or missing information), which is sometimes the case. However, to highlight this methodological difference, the classification is based on ABCD and not on the current ABC D1/D2 classification, which, for the unexplained category, corresponds to a stronger validation of the unexplained nature of the case. Here, the case is on the borderline between an unexplained case and a case that cannot be investigated due to a lack of consistency in the case file, resulting from the absence of an on-site GEIPAN investigation. Consequently, the case is classified as D: unexplained.

summary: Observation in the night sky of the straight (or slightly curved) and silent passage of a luminous phenomenon of color (white then yellow-orange or red) which seems to approach the witnesses as they grow larger: probable observation of an aircraft.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, classified at the time (A, B, C, or D), which are now being re-examined solely to refine the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even a change in classification. This case of observation (also known as VRIGNES AUX BOIS (08) 1980) was revisited in 2007 and classified as Class C, and has been recently re-examined (see the investigation report). On March 11, 1980, around 9:00 PM, a motorist (T1) was alerted by his young son (T2) to the presence in the sky of a luminous phenomenon "like a star." It appeared to be approaching and changing from the size of a coin to that of a plate, which frightened the witnesses. Panicked, the motorist turned around, and his son told him that the point had turned red. The vehicle's engine then stalled, and the light went out. The vehicle eventually restarted after several attempts. The phenomenon then passed over the vehicle and gradually moved away. The frightened witnesses returned home. They. No particular noise was heard. The driver went to the police station at 10:30 p.m., and an investigation was launched on site at 11:40 p.m.: no traces were found on the ground or vegetation. No other statements were collected. The witnesses likely observed an aircraft approaching them, with its landing light(s) or searchlight (helicopter) illuminated. This powerful light prevented the visual perception of any other lights. Only the left navigation light was briefly glimpsed by T2, either temporarily or at the end of the observation, before the UFO was lost from sight. No noise was perceived, but this parameter is not conclusive. It depends on many factors, such as the witnesses' own auditory perception, the distance of the phenomenon, and any noises present inside the car. All these parameters being unknown. as well as the wind strength and direction. And above all, when the witness states, "I didn't hear the slightest noise from the phenomenon at (PV)," they do not specify whether the observation was made with the vehicle window open or closed. We have demonstrated throughout the investigation that the visibility conditions inside the witnesses' vehicles considerably limited their field of vision and that the observation was made while the UFO remained visually low on the horizon, even after the U-turn. It was therefore probably still very far from the witnesses when they made the U-turn and, in the panic and stress, triggered a chain of events unrelated to the phenomenon itself (engine stalling, lights going out, flashlight not working). The witnesses are completely consumed by their stress and the desire to leave the observation site, the UFO, as quickly as possible, always under the assumption of confusion with a The aircraft, still far from the witnesses, had ample opportunity to disappear completely from their field of vision, possibly due to a turn. T1 (the driver) claims to have seen the red dot of the UFO again, as my son had said, in front of him. We were able to show that this red dot, observed at that moment, was probably only the planet Mars, visible in conjunction with the planet Jupiter, in the direction of observation (southeast), facing the witnesses. Panicked and thinking only of getting home at that moment, T1 did not dwell further on this final observation of Mars, which was probably very brief, preventing him from noticing that this red dot was not moving and therefore could not be linked to the UFO. The witness's need to try to concentrate on his driving, at night and on a road in poor condition, due to his state of stress, reinforces this point. The rapid and gradual disappearance of Mars could have been the cause of the accident. This was likely caused by a thick bank of fog passing in front of the planet, the presence of which is confirmed by meteorological data. This disappearance contributes to the illusion of the UFO because the decrease in intensity can be interpreted as an increase in the UFO's distance. This final confusion with the planet Mars invalidates the second part of the UFO's trajectory as presented in the two sources of information relating to the case, after its passage over the witnesses' vehicle. They would ultimately have observed it only in a northwesterly direction. Regarding the related phenomena of engine stalling and the simultaneous extinction of the car's lights, we have shown that a malfunction causing the immediate and total shutdown of both the engine and the lights is highly improbable, given the mechanical and electrical design of the witness's vehicle. The hypothesis that the stalling was caused by driver inattention on the part of T1, who was under considerable stress at that moment, is more likely. It is by It is also conceivable that, as an unconscious reflex of fear and self-preservation (to avoid being spotted), the witness deliberately turned off his lights and then turned them back on. The fear of ridicule, upon reflection, could explain why T1 did not wish to mention it explicitly to the investigators. However, this remains highly hypothetical, as no concrete evidence supports this hypothesis. In light of all these points, it now seems inappropriate to link the two events. The first was probably simply an aircraft observed under particular conditions (at night and head-on, with one or more landing lights or a searchlight illuminated), which triggered a cascade of panic reactions from both witnesses, who were in a state of extreme stress. The consistency of the evidence is moderate. Data is lacking, including angular measurements (apparent dimensions of the UFO) and testimonial information (open or closed windows, T2's position in the aircraft). The passenger compartment (T2's testimony) and photographs (no photos or videos of the phenomenon). The absence of this data makes it impossible to either refute or firmly support the aircraft hypothesis, which nevertheless remains sufficiently probable to be considered. Classification D (which existed for a time for this case) is, however, excluded due to this hypothesis, which reduces its strangeness. GEIPAN classifies it as B: probable observation of an aircraft.

summary: Observation of a large rectangular shape with light ramps.
description: On March 10, 1980, at the end of their shift, the gendarmes of the Authon-du-Perche brigade received a call from the neighboring brigade reporting a taxi driver who had seen a strange light on the road to Authon. They quickly went to the scene but found nothing unusual. Back home, one of the gendarmes and his wife continued to watch the sky, and around 10:15 p.m., they spotted a light larger than a star, moving erratically across the sky. This light was in the shape of an orange disc. The gendarme called his colleagues, and the four of them set off in a car to search for the curious phenomenon. After following it and losing sight of it several times due to the terrain, they finally got out of the car at an intersection. They then observed a large rectangular shape with rounded corners and white light beams illuminating the surrounding landscape and the car. One of the officers felt a sensation of heat and a strong feeling of fear that later prevented him from sleeping. The officers returned home around 11:30 p.m. No explanation could be found for this sighting, the characteristics of which—erratic and very rapid movements—are also found in other eyewitness accounts.

summary: Probable observation of Mars
description: On March 4, 1980, at approximately 9:45 PM, numerous witnesses reported observing a luminous phenomenon five times larger and brighter than a star. This sphere was reddish-orange in color and remained stationary in the sky. The investigation revealed that the conditions were exceptionally favorable for observing certain planets, such as Mars, in a very particular light.

summary: successive observations of distinct luminous phenomena.
description: On March 3rd and 7th, 1980, several people observed unusual and distinct luminous phenomena. On March 3rd at 10:15 PM, a driver and her daughter were suddenly dazzled by a red light emanating from a sphere moving close to the horizon. This sphere, about the size of a soccer ball, moved silently from southeast to northwest. Its movement appeared to be in stages and at high speed. This phenomenon was also observed by others, including the police, who at 10:25 PM saw a large, bright reddish point, five degrees above the horizon, which slowly disappeared at 10:35 PM in the northwest. These officers returned to the area the following day and observed, through binoculars, an orange luminous object emitting bluish flashes. This object disappeared completely over the horizon at 10:45 PM. It should be noted that at this time of year, Venus was particularly visible (magnitude -4.10) and very low on the horizon (less than 5 arcseconds above the horizon) and disappeared completely around 10:38 PM. The speed and gradual descent reported by witnesses is an impression given by the fact that the celestial body was very low and very far on the horizon. The witnesses probably made an astronomical observation of Venus that evening. On March 7, 1980, around 10:10 PM, these same people and others witnessed another unusual luminous phenomenon. Returning home and getting out of her car, a witness observed a luminous sphere made up of different colored circles. A flash struck the ground at her child's feet. The sphere, with an estimated diameter of between 20 and 25 cm, moved from west to northwest before disappearing completely. No sound was heard and no electric shock was felt. However, a drop in voltage on the EDF power line will be observed by many people in their homes or on streetlights: it should also be noted that one of the witnesses mentions an electrical arc seen between a power line and the ground. These people have probably witnessed an electrical phenomenon.

summary: probable observation of Venus.
description: On March 3, 1980, starting at 8:45 PM and lasting for half an hour, witnesses observed a luminous sphere shaped like a plate above the mountain ridges. According to the witnesses, this object was located between 100 and 200 meters from their vehicle. When the car stopped, the witnesses heard no noise and smelled no unusual odor. Over a distance of approximately 12 kilometers, these individuals had the impression that the object was following them, as it seemed to stop and start moving at the same time as their vehicle. The object suddenly disappeared, and another luminous phenomenon, this time red and conical, appeared. Upon returning home, the witnesses went to the gendarmerie to file a report. No other witnesses or traces of the phenomenon were found during the investigation. Based on the route taken by the witnesses between Favello and Corte, and considering the very winding road between these two places, it is likely that these people made an astronomical observation of Venus. Particularly visible at this time of year (magnitude -4.10) and very low on the horizon, this celestial body would have appeared and disappeared following the ridgeline.

summary: Sighting of an orange ball on the horizon: probable sighting of the moon
description: On March 3, 1980, between 8:30 and 8:45 PM, a couple driving by observed an orange orb the size of the setting sun. A little later, they could no longer see this orb, but they did notice the presence of the moon, which appeared whiter. It is likely that the witnesses were surprised by the unusual appearance of the moon at the beginning of the night, illuminated by the setting sun.

summary: Observations of a luminous object of varying color intensity at low altitude in the night sky: observations of Venus at sunset.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. These publications include older cases, originally classified as type B, which are now being re-examined solely to improve the relevance of the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience gained over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This case, previously classified as type B and named COUCY LE CHÂTEAU (02) 1980, is part of a set of re-examined cases (see the investigation report). On March 2, 1980, between 9:45 PM and 10:00 PM, four witnesses in Saint-Paul-aux-Bois observed a luminous object in the direction of Salency (02). The object's brightness and color varied. Three witnesses (T1, T2, T3) reported the object moving along a downward trajectory. T4 reported it as stationary. The police, called at 9:55 PM, went to the scene immediately but found nothing unusual in the western sky. This case is quite consistent (four witnesses), and the description of the observed UFO is fairly precise. The witnesses' sincerity and credibility have never been questioned. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, shape, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: Venus at sunset. Furthermore, Venus was setting on the horizon in the direction indicated by the witnesses. It is not the visual perception of the witnesses that is the issue, but rather their interpretation of their observation through their feelings (fatigue, surprise). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of weak strangeness is classified as UAP A, an observation linked to a misinterpretation of Venus at sunset.

summary: observation of several bright spots
description: On February 29, 1980, between 8:30 PM and 9:40 PM, two witnesses repeatedly observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon. An object composed of several spheres moved very high in the sky. This object resembled a brooch of several bluish and pinkish spheres. The overall shape was oval, and on the right side, a larger, flashing light was noticed. No noise was heard during the observations. As it moved, the object took the form of a luminous bar and then disappeared abruptly. No further information was gathered about this phenomenon, for which we lack data.

summary: Moon observation
description: On February 24, 1980, at approximately 3:15 a.m., a group of young people spotted an orange glow through the fir trees near the beach. Moving to get a better view, they saw a very large object heading towards the Île d'Yeu. It was three-quarters spherical, orange in color, and lacked any shine. This craft was moving vertically at a very slow and constant speed. The observation, which lasted about ten minutes, ended when the object slowly sank into the ocean, leaving a whitish glow. No sound was heard. At approximately 3:05 a.m., a gendarme on patrol also spotted a hemispherical object, larger than a crescent moon, reddish-orange in color and lacking any shine. This object was moving slowly and descending vertically without changing shape or color. All these people made an astronomical observation of the setting moon (at exactly 3:12 AM), noting its size and orange color. Furthermore, the moon was in its first quarter, which gave it the appearance of a downward-facing half-disc.

summary: Observation of the Moon and Venus
description: On February 18, 1980, several people observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon from the courtyard of a house, surrounded by a hazy halo. A whitish, luminous sphere remained motionless near another object resembling a crescent moon. This observation lasted several minutes, after which the phenomenon began to move from side to side and up and down for about twenty minutes. The object then moved at high speed along a northwest trajectory. Its volume appeared three times larger than the surrounding celestial bodies, and it shone brighter. It gradually disappeared as it moved away. No noise was heard during the observation. No other reports were collected about this phenomenon. However, a few days later, the local press reported the observation of an "earthshine," an ashen light that accompanies the new moon and can be accompanied by particular visual effects when atmospheric disturbances are present. Examining the star chart suggests that this was an astronomical observation. Indeed, the Moon (magnitude -7.70) is visible until 9:02 PM and then dips below the horizon. On this date (the new moon is on the 16th), only a thin crescent is visible. Venus is located just above the Moon (magnitude -4.19). Furthermore, the phenomenon of Earthshine (or ashen light) is visible when the Earth, Moon, and Sun are almost aligned. From our planet, the Moon appears as a very thin crescent, but the Earth, as seen from our satellite, is full and shines brightly. It is Earthshine that makes the unlit portion of the Moon glow very faintly. After the new moon, the phenomenon is observable in the evening from the third to the fifth day, and before the new moon, it is visible in the morning from the fifth to the third day before the next lunar cycle. Therefore, we can safely say that the main witness, who made the observation around, and rather before, 9:00 PM, saw the moon (with an Earthrise) and Venus just above it. The police officers who made the observation at 9:15 PM saw Venus before it too disappeared below the horizon, the moon having already disappeared for about twelve minutes. It is true that the witnesses reported "rapid" movements and a rapid displacement before disappearance. It is likely that the witnesses unconsciously exaggerated these movements, due to the proximity of the horizon and perhaps also a phenomenon of "autokinetic motion" (the impression of movement when one stares intently at something).

summary: Probable observation of the planet Venus
description: On February 17, 1980, at approximately 8:45 PM, a witness observing the sky spotted a very bright point that intrigued him. This round point was stationary, larger, and yellower than the other stars. The observation lasted more than 10 minutes without the point appearing to move. The police were unable to locate any witnesses to provide further information. However, the local press reported that other witnesses in the area had made the same observation. After checking a star chart, we noted that in the indicated direction, Venus is particularly visible (magnitude -4.01) at this time of year. Venus's altitude above the horizon was 8 arcseconds instead of the 20 arcseconds indicated by the witness. Taking into account a possible margin of error regarding the object's altitude, the most likely hypothesis is a sighting of Venus. Numerous sightings were reported during this period.

summary: observation of luminous orbs and close encounter of the 3rd kind.
description: witness recounts seeing white orbs three times since the beginning of 1980. Each time, these orbs seemed to follow the vehicle as it traveled at night. They could leave a white trail when they disappeared. In the presence of his friend, they saw an orb together near a house. The witness also describes an encounter in his vehicle with an entity that allegedly told him it had contacted him three times and warned him of an invasion of Earth. He describes a tall, handsome man with blue eyes and long hair. The witness speaks of a half-hour memory loss and arrived at his parents' house in a state of shock. Taken home, his condition was confirmed the next day by a doctor. No other witnesses have been found, and no other information has been gathered about these phenomena that would corroborate this testimony.

summary: Observation of an object moving in stages.
description: On February 16, 1980, between 1:00 and 1:30 a.m., three on-duty military personnel reported observing an unidentified flying object. This object was flying over the village. According to the witnesses, who differed on the object's shape, it emitted an intense orange light. It remained stationary for a minute before rapidly ascending and moving in stages. The intensity of the light gradually decreased until it became a point. No further information was gathered from civilians in the area. As no radar surveillance had been conducted over the weekend, confirmation of the presence of an aircraft could not be made. This case is classified as Class C due to lack of data.

summary: probable observation of Venus
description: At approximately 8:35 PM on February 15, 1980, a witness observed a luminous sphere to the southwest. It was located directly above a building. Leaning against a wall to observe the phenomenon through binoculars, the witness noted the presence of two spheres. These, one red and one white located above the first, were moving without actually moving. The positions of the two spheres reversed, and the entire object disappeared after tracing a fairly wide "Z" shape across the sky. The observation lasted about 10 minutes under a perfectly clear sky. No other witnesses to this phenomenon, for which we lack data, came forward to the police. This witness likely made an astronomical observation of Venus (magnitude -4), very low on the horizon, which then disappeared into the urban landscape.

summary: Motorist observing a glow the shape and size of a half-moon: probable sighting of the Moon.
description: On February 13, 1980, at approximately 5:40 a.m., a postal worker on his way to work spotted a luminous phenomenon in a clear sky that intrigued him. Above the Monts du Lyonnais region, he observed a crescent-shaped glow for eight minutes. It was yellow-orange in color and moved slowly along a north-south trajectory. This glow gradually faded. Only another witness who was with the postal worker saw the phenomenon; however, he did not file a report with the police. An examination of the star chart for that period shows the moon very faint (new moon on the 16th) and very low on the horizon, but in the direction of the observation. The witness stated that there was no moon: in fact, he probably observed its glow without recognizing it (magnitude -8.9).

summary: Observation of a spherical craft following the witness.
description: On January 28, 1980, at approximately 4:15 a.m., a witness driving a car noticed a luminous object to his right. This spherical object was stationary about 40 meters above the ground and 150 meters from the witness. Orange in color, it emitted a bright light directed towards the sky. This object was itself contained within a larger, brighter circle. The witness continued driving and noticed that the object seemed to be following him. The witness noticed no noise or odor, which frightened him. The object disappeared into the landscape shortly afterward. No other witnesses or information have been gathered about this phenomenon, for which we lack details.

summary: Probable observations of the planet Venus.
description: On January 27, 1980, between 9:05 PM and 9:10 PM, several witnesses observed a bright orange ball in a clear sky. Located low on the horizon, it appeared to blink intermittently. The observation lasted 10 to 15 minutes for some witnesses. A similar observation occurred the following day. A review of the star chart suggests that these reports are likely related to the observation of Venus, visible in the west-southwest with a high magnitude of -3.9, which disappeared below the horizon around 9:10 PM.

summary: Probable observation of celestial bodies
description: On January 25, 1980, around 10 p.m., a witness and the police officers called to the scene observed two bright points of light, brighter than the stars. These two points slowly rose in the sky throughout the evening and were visible in the following days when the sky was clear. This was probably a celestial observation.

summary: Probable observations of atmospheric re-entries.
description: On January 23 and 24, 1980, unusual luminous phenomena were observed over the ocean in Martinique and Guadeloupe. From various locations on the islands, between 6 and 7 p.m., witnesses saw one or more luminous objects, sometimes followed by trails of multicolored lights. The sky was clear, and according to the witnesses, who only saw these phenomena for a few seconds, the objects disappeared rapidly as they moved. Based on the different descriptions, the prevailing hypothesis is that of probable atmospheric reentry.

summary: A hoax about a witness being abducted by aliens is staged for publicity purposes.
description: On February 22, 1980, while reading the weekly magazine "SPECIAL DERNIERE" No. 572, dated February 15-21, 1980, the police learned that the husband of a restaurant owner had allegedly been abducted by extraterrestrials. The supposed event had taken place on January 21, 1980, around 9:00 a.m. in the Vierzon forest. The police investigation quickly concluded that the hoax had been completely fabricated and was admitted by the witness.

summary: Observation of a luminous, oval flying object.
description: On January 24, 1980, between 6:05 PM and 6:25 PM, a witness reported seeing an unidentified flying object arrive and depart. Initially, he described the object as cylindrical with two small, dark-colored fins on its side. As the object approached, it stabilized at an altitude of 200 meters and was then located approximately 300 meters east of a water tower. The witness then noticed that the object was oval-shaped, illuminated by a bright yellow-orange light, and that the fins had disappeared. During the seven-minute observation, the witness noticed his radio was crackling abnormally and he scanned the area several times with a portable spotlight. The object suddenly moved away, rapidly gaining altitude. The frightened witness went to alert the police. A malfunction in the electrical circuit of the vehicle's dashboard will be observed. No further information will be gathered regarding this unexplained phenomenon.

summary: Probable observation of Venus.
description: On January 16, 1980, at 7:00 PM, witnesses observed a peculiar luminous phenomenon in the sky. It was a very bright white sphere located in the southwest. During observation, the phenomenon changed color and brightness, and appeared to shrink or grow; threads seemed to descend from the object. None of the witnesses heard any noise during the entire observation. The phenomenon moved away rapidly and was lost from sight around 9:00 PM. One of the witnesses took photographs, but the film was black and showed nothing. According to the gendarmerie's investigation at the meteorological station, no French weather balloons had been launched or reported in the area. It should be noted, however, that a few days earlier, a foreign weather balloon had been discovered in another municipality. According to the star chart, Venus was particularly visible at that time (magnitude -3.84) and low on the southwest horizon. It also disappears around 9 p.m. These people were probably observing Venus.

summary: Sighting of a saucer-shaped craft.
description: On January 13, 1980, at approximately 7:10 a.m., a motorist passing through Charente-Maritime spotted a saucer-shaped object. Stationary, the object was about 5 to 6 meters in diameter, and lights were flashing at its extremities. Getting out of his vehicle, the witness, a customs officer, observed the craft slowly moving away at about 30 to 40 km/h. What astonished the witness was that during the five minutes of observation, he heard no noise coming from the craft. The witness, in a hurry, gave his statement upon arriving in Haute-Garonne. No other witnesses came forward in the area of the sighting, and no further information was gathered about this phenomenon, which remains unexplained.

summary: observation of Venus
description: Between January 10th and 16th, 1980, numerous people, including police officers, observed a luminous object in the sky. Circular in shape, it was bright and shimmering. It moved slowly from east to west. Photographs of the object were taken. Gradually, the object lost its brightness, turning orange and disappearing. All these people made an astronomical observation of Venus, which was particularly visible at that time of year (magnitude -3.83 on January 12th, 1980 at 7:04 PM and disappearance over the ocean at 8:30 PM).

summary: Observation of the planet Venus
description: On January 5, 1980, starting at 6:30 PM, several witnesses observed a luminous phenomenon that intrigued them. A sphere emitting an intense light was initially motionless, then moved slowly and silently across the clear sky. The colors and size varied according to the witnesses. For some, it appeared to be rotating on its own axis. The witnesses' positions and direction of observation placed the phenomenon in the southwest. The phenomenon disappeared around 7:30 PM. Examination of the star chart for that date and time shows that the witnesses simply observed the planet Venus, which was particularly visible and bright at that time of year (magnitude -3.8). Venus sets at 7:30 PM, as indicated by the witnesses.

summary: A multi-colored glow was observed in the sky: a possible sighting of the planet Venus.
description: Starting on January 5, 1980, and in the days that followed, numerous witnesses, as well as the gendarmes investigating the incident, observed a very bright glow in the sky in the late afternoon. Its shape and colors appeared to change. There was a strong likelihood that the observation was of Venus.

summary: probable observation of the full moon reddened by the rising sun
description: On the morning of January 3, 1980, at 8:05 a.m., a witness, closing his shutters, spotted a red ball in the sky. This ball disappeared behind clouds and then reappeared. It moved irregularly and at a very rapid speed. The reported trajectory was southeast to northwest. When his neighbor called out to him, she did not see the object. The witness took photographs, and the police were able to examine the negative, which showed a brown spot. To this day, the negative has not been found in the archives. No other witness accounts of this phenomenon have been collected. The witness likely made an astronomical observation of the full moon, which, at the indicated time, was setting and illuminated by the rising sun, giving the moon its red color.

summary: Periodic observation of a luminous ball moving slowly along a straight line.
description: On January 1, 1980, several military personnel on duty observed a luminous phenomenon in the sky on three separate occasions. A small orange ball appeared suddenly and successively at 11:16 PM, 11:33 PM, and 11:46 PM. An intense glow accompanied this object, which moved slowly and always along a horizontal trajectory. Each time it appeared in the same location, the dogs in the base's kennel howled in terror. No noise or smoke accompanied the object's movement, and the military personnel were certain it was not light emitted by an airplane or helicopter. No civilians witnessed this phenomenon, which remains unexplained.

summary: Observation of a stationary point of light in the sky: mistaken for Venus.
description: GEIPAN continues to publish its entire archive on its public website www.geipan.fr. Among its publications are older cases, originally classified as type C, which are now being re-examined solely to improve the relevance of the conclusions. Thanks to new technical resources (software) and the investigative experience acquired over the years, this re-examination sometimes leads to new observations or even an explicit change in classification in an investigation report. This particular observation is one of the cases classified as type C in 1980 by GEIPAN. On January 1, 1980, between 6:30 and 7:00 PM, a motorist traveling eastbound on the A8 motorway observed a bright, stationary point of light in the clear sky, facing west. Observation through binoculars allowed the witness to describe this very bright point as a ball of string, revealing black squares between the strands. The witness took photographs of the phenomenon, but the negatives later handed over to the police were transparent and devoid of any image. No other witness statements were collected regarding this phenomenon. The described phenomenon shares many characteristics (duration of observation, size, color) with a well-known astronomical object: the planet Venus. Furthermore, Venus was indeed present in the observed area of the sky, even though the witness made no mention of it. It is not the witness's visual perception that is at issue, but rather the witness's interpretation of the observation based on their feelings (astonishment, night driving). In the current GEIPAN classification, this case of a weak anomaly is classified as UAP A, an observation linked to a misidentification of Venus.

summary: Observation of a luminous phenomenon.
description: In July 2008, a witness reported a nighttime sighting in 1980 or 1981, accompanied by two family members, on the northbound carriageway of the Lyon-Avignon motorway. For approximately thirty seconds, they observed a luminous sphere that then split into three stationary entities before disappearing into the sky at very high speed. Our requests for further information (particularly regarding the date, which is given arbitrarily) have gone unanswered to date, and we lack further details and information about this sighting.
